occupation.title: Medical assistant and patient-care support worker
occupation.organization: A community outpatient clinic in San Antonio
occupation.annual_income_context: His base pay is close to the roughly $38,220 annual wage figure commonly reported for healthcare support work. Occasional overtime and weekend coverage can bring his gross earnings to around $40,000–$42,000 in a busier year. His household income remains below $50,000 and is tight after rent, childcare, transportation, and insurance costs.
occupation.description: Andrés works in a busy outpatient clinic that sees families, older adults, and patients managing chronic conditions. He brings patients to examination rooms, records vital signs, confirms medication lists, updates electronic charts, prepares rooms, keeps basic supplies stocked, and helps patients understand where to go next. Depending on the day, he may assist with simple clinical procedures within his training and clinic policy, relay patient concerns to a nurse, or help calm someone who is nervous about an appointment. He is careful not to present himself as a clinician or offer advice beyond his role. He has a steady manner with patients who are embarrassed, confused, or impatient, and coworkers often ask him to explain a process in plain language.
occupation.workplace_realities: The pace is uneven: an apparently calm morning can become crowded when appointments run late or several walk-ins arrive together. Andrés likes being useful but dislikes being expected to absorb every delay without a break. He is conscientious about patient privacy and handoffs, although he sometimes has to remind himself to slow down when he is trying to finish tasks before school pickup. He generally works weekday shifts beginning in the morning, with occasional early starts, late coverage, or Saturdays. A schedule change can create an immediate childcare problem, so he tries to ask for notice and trades shifts when possible.
occupation.strengths_and_limitations: He is reliable with practical patient-care tasks, communicates warmly, and notices when someone has not understood an instruction. He is less comfortable with advanced billing rules, complicated insurance questions, or lengthy administrative forms. He is considering further training but has not committed to a specific program because tuition, time, and childcare would all have to work.

interests: Reading books in short sessions before bed or while waiting for Mateo.
Listening to audiobooks during a commute or while doing laundry.
Crime novels and mysteries with believable characters.
Memoirs about family, work, or growing up between languages and cultures.
Accessible history books, especially when they connect to a place or family story.
Occasional science fiction that is more character-focused than technical.
Children's picture books with humor, rhythm, and illustrations Mateo wants to revisit.
Finding used books at library sales, thrift shops, or neighborhood book exchanges.
San Antonio neighborhood events and local food spots.
Baseball on the radio or television when he has a quiet evening.
College and professional sports, mostly as a casual fan rather than a statistics devotee.
Cooking familiar meals and trying one new recipe when time allows.
Parks, splash pads, and low-cost outings with his son.
Music for driving, including Latin pop, Tejano, old-school R&B, and mainstream country.
Short practical videos that show a repair or household task step by step.
Stories from his mother and aunts about relatives and earlier generations.
Learning medical vocabulary and small work-related skills that make his job easier.
Watching a comedy or a crime series after Mateo is asleep.
Walking around a store or outdoor market without needing to make a big event of it.
Collecting a few favorite children's books to read again rather than constantly buying new ones.
likes: A book that can be picked up after several days without losing the thread.
Paperback books with readable print and pages that do not feel too delicate to carry in a backpack.
A good audiobook narrator who sounds natural rather than theatrical.
Reading aloud with Mateo, especially when Mateo joins in on repeated phrases.
A clear, direct explanation from a nurse or supervisor instead of jargon.
People who give practical help without making him feel indebted or judged.
A quiet half hour after Mateo goes to bed, even if he only reads a few pages.
Strong coffee in the morning, usually inexpensive and taken on the way to work.
Breakfast tacos, especially when there is time to sit down and eat them warm.
Beans, rice, grilled chicken, caldo, and other familiar home-cooked meals.
Fresh tortillas and the smell of food cooking at his mother's house.
A cool evening after a very hot day.
Clean sheets and a reasonably uncluttered kitchen counter.
A clinic coworker who notices when the room is falling behind and helps without keeping score.
Text messages that state the pickup time or plan plainly.
A park visit that does not require tickets, reservations, or a long drive.
Mateo asking to hear the same story again.
Family gatherings that are relaxed enough for people to drift in and out.
Music that makes a long drive feel shorter.
Being treated as a competent parent rather than praised as if ordinary caregiving were surprising.
dislikes: Being rushed to make a decision while someone is talking over him.
Medical bills that arrive with unclear explanations or surprise balances.
Forms that repeat information he has already entered several times.
People who assume he cannot understand a conversation because he uses Spanish with family.
People who assume he is fluent in every kind of Spanish or expect him to translate complex medical information.
Being told to simply budget better when the problem is that basic expenses already take most of his income.
Last-minute work schedule changes that disrupt school pickup.
A long phone hold when he is trying to resolve an insurance or childcare issue.
Condescending comments about single fathers or about his family arrangement.
Noisy television or phone audio while he is trying to read.
Books that depend on a huge cast of characters introduced all at once.
Finishing a book only because someone says it is important, when it is not holding his attention.
Overly competitive parenting conversations.
Food waste, especially when groceries are expensive.
Traffic that makes an already narrow pickup window stressful.
People who treat a missed appointment as proof that someone does not care.
Being pressured to discuss his child's mother in front of people who do not know the situation.
Aggressive political arguments that leave no room for practical disagreement.
A packed weekend with no chance to rest or catch up on laundry.
Advice that assumes he has a flexible schedule, a spare car, or money set aside for every emergency.

reading_habits.motivation: He genuinely likes books, but reading is intermittent because work, parenting, and household tasks divide his attention. He often reads ten or fifteen minutes at a time, puts a book down for several days, and then returns to it.
reading_habits.formats: Mostly paperbacks borrowed from the library or bought used, with occasional e-books and audiobooks. Audio is especially useful when his hands are busy, though he sometimes has to rewind after being interrupted.
reading_habits.genres_and_choices: Chooses mysteries, crime fiction, memoirs, accessible history, and the occasional science-fiction novel. He is more likely to finish a book with clear chapters, a strong voice, and characters he can keep straight.
reading_habits.family_reading: He tries to read aloud with Mateo several nights a week, though the routine is not perfectly consistent. Mateo sometimes chooses the same picture book repeatedly; Andrés accepts repetition as part of the ritual.

traits: Warm and considerate in ordinary interactions, especially toward children, older adults, and people who seem embarrassed to ask for help.
Cooperative by default, but increasingly willing to say no when a request would interfere with his son's needs or his own rest.
Flexible when plans change; he can improvise a meal, find a different pickup arrangement, or adjust a weekend without dwelling on the original plan.
Spontaneous in small ways, such as accepting an invitation or taking Mateo to a park on short notice, but less comfortable with large, complicated plans.
Sometimes weak on follow-through when a task is not urgent, particularly paperwork, personal appointments, or studying after a long shift.
Quietly proud of being dependable and sensitive to criticism that implies he is careless or not doing enough as a father.
Patient with people in distress, but more irritable when hungry, sleep-deprived, or trying to solve several practical problems at once.
Funny in a dry, affectionate way; he often uses a small joke to take the edge off a tense moment rather than to command attention.
Protective without wanting to control his son; he tries to let Mateo try things while keeping a close eye on safety.
Practical and resourceful, with a preference for solutions that can be acted on today over abstract advice that assumes unlimited time or money.
Socially open with familiar people but not someone who immediately tells strangers personal details.
Capable of setting a boundary once he has thought it through, though he may initially agree and later realize he has taken on too much.
Feels stress physically and mentally; a series of small setbacks can make him feel cornered even when each one is manageable on its own.
Accepts help more readily from trusted relatives than from institutions, partly because asking for assistance can feel exposing.
Not rigid about traditions or political labels; he is willing to revise an opinion when he hears a credible personal experience or sees a practical reason.

big_five.openness: Moderate. He enjoys books, stories, new foods, and learning useful skills, but tends to prefer ideas connected to everyday life over novelty for its own sake.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate, with a strong sense of responsibility toward patients and his son but uneven organization in personal tasks. He uses reminders and routines when the stakes are high, yet can procrastinate on forms or long-term planning.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate-low. He is friendly and can work comfortably with a steady stream of people, but needs quiet time after a demanding shift and does not seek out large social gatherings.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. He is accommodating, empathetic, and cooperative, though he can be direct when a boundary, patient-safety issue, or parenting matter is involved.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate-high under sustained pressure. He worries about money, childcare, and letting people down; he is not constantly anxious, but uncertainty and accumulating expenses can make him feel overwhelmed.

beliefs: A child should feel loved and safe even when the adults raising them do not live together.
Showing up consistently matters more than making grand promises.
A parent who asks relatives for help is still a capable parent.
Children benefit from clear limits, but discipline should not rely on humiliation or fear.
Mateo should be allowed to ask questions about his family without being made responsible for adult feelings.
It is valuable for Mateo to hear Spanish at home, even if his own Spanish is imperfect.
Language is a living family connection, not a test that Mateo has to pass.
Family traditions are worth keeping when they bring people together, but they can change as families change.
Respect for elders matters, but it does not require agreeing with everything an older relative says.
People deserve to be treated with dignity regardless of their income, accent, immigration history, or job title.
Healthcare workers in support roles contribute meaningfully to patient care even when their work is not highly visible.
Patients should be able to understand what is happening to them in plain language.
Privacy is especially important when someone is sharing health information.
A person should not be judged as irresponsible based on one missed appointment or an incomplete form.
Healthcare is too expensive for many working people, and a job with insurance does not automatically make care affordable.
Preventive care is worthwhile, but cost can make it difficult to follow through.
People should be able to seek mental health support without being treated as weak.
Employers should give workers reasonable notice of schedule changes, especially when workers have caregiving duties.
A reliable childcare arrangement is part of what makes employment possible, not an optional luxury.
Public schools, libraries, and after-school programs provide important support to working families.
Economic inequality is a real problem, and individual effort alone cannot erase high housing, healthcare, and childcare costs.
Public services should be accessible and practical, not designed only for people with flexible jobs and reliable transportation.
Workers should be paid fairly for the responsibility and physical effort their jobs require.
He generally supports civil rights and social inclusion, while sometimes feeling uncertain about the details of policies he has not studied closely.
He dislikes political loyalty tests and can agree with people on one issue while disagreeing with them on another.
Public safety matters, but he does not think every social problem can be solved by punishment alone.
People should be able to disagree without turning a conversation into a judgment about someone's whole character.
Faith can offer comfort and a sense of continuity, but people should not use religion to shame others.
He identifies as Catholic, though his practice is occasional and more connected to family milestones, holidays, and personal reflection than a strict weekly routine.
Prayer is something he may turn to when worried, but he also believes people should make practical plans and ask for help.
Books can give a person company and perspective even when there is not enough time to read regularly.
Reading with a child is valuable for connection as well as vocabulary or school readiness.
Being a good father does not mean never getting frustrated; it means noticing, repairing, and trying again.
A stable home is more about reliability, care, and safety than about having expensive possessions.
It is sensible to plan for the future, but plans need room for emergencies and changing circumstances.
skills: Taking and documenting routine vital signs accurately within his training and workplace protocols.
Preparing examination rooms and restocking commonly used supplies.
Patient intake, including confirming basic information and listening for concerns that need to be passed to a nurse or clinician.
Using electronic health record systems for routine chart updates and documentation.
Explaining ordinary clinic steps in calm, plain language without pretending to make clinical decisions.
Keeping patient information private in conversations and at the workstation.
Recognizing when a patient seems confused, anxious, or uncomfortable and checking whether they need additional assistance.
Managing several small tasks during a busy clinic shift while trying to preserve accurate handoffs.
De-escalating everyday tension through patience, a steady voice, and practical choices.
Conversational Spanish for familiar family and community interactions, with awareness of his limits in complex or technical interpretation.
Coordinating school pickup, aftercare, family help, and work shifts through phone calendars and reminder alarms.
Preparing inexpensive meals from basic groceries and adapting when an ingredient is missing.
Basic household troubleshooting, including simple furniture assembly and minor fixes that do not require a licensed professional.
Learning procedures by observing experienced coworkers and repeating the task under appropriate supervision.
Reading aloud expressively enough to hold a young child's attention, including making up voices for characters.
Finding library resources, used books, and low-cost activities for his son.
Driving confidently in city traffic and planning alternate routes when roads are congested.
Asking for clarification when a work instruction or school message is unclear, although he may wait longer than ideal if he feels rushed.

relationships.name: Mateo Montoya
relationships.description: Mateo is Andrés's only child and the center of his daily life. He is energetic, talkative when comfortable, and currently interested in picture books, toy vehicles, and asking repeated why questions. Andrés handles most daily care, school communication, appointments, meals, and bedtime. He tries to be affectionate and dependable while learning not to overreact when the ordinary chaos of a five-year-old catches him at the end of a tiring day.

relationships.name: Lucía
relationships.relationship: Mateo's mother and Andrés's former partner
relationships.description: Andrés and Lucía never married and are no longer a couple. She has contact with Mateo and participates in some scheduled visits and decisions, but Andrés manages most of the everyday caregiving. Their communication is generally civil and focused on Mateo, though they sometimes disagree about timing, expenses, or how much notice a schedule change requires. Andrés tries to keep adult frustration out of conversations with Mateo.

relationships.name: Elena Montoya
relationships.description: Elena lives nearby and is one of his most dependable sources of help. She sometimes picks Mateo up, watches him for a few hours, or sends food home. She is affectionate and involved, and her support makes Andrés's work schedule more manageable. They occasionally disagree about parenting choices, but he trusts her and tries to speak up respectfully rather than letting resentment build.

relationships.name: Rosa
relationships.description: Rosa is a backup caregiver for occasional school closures or appointment conflicts. She is practical and good at making Mateo feel welcome, but she has her own responsibilities and cannot be treated as guaranteed childcare.

relationships.name: Darnell
relationships.relationship: Close friend from an earlier job
relationships.description: Darnell checks in by text, shares occasional meals with Andrés, and is someone Andrés can admit to when he is having a rough week. They do not see each other often because of work and parenting schedules, but their friendship is comfortable and not dependent on constant contact.

relationships.name: Clinic colleagues
relationships.description: He has a few coworkers he trusts for practical advice about clinic routines, schedule swaps, and difficult patient interactions. He is friendly with the wider staff but keeps his personal life private until he knows someone well.

relationships.name: School teacher and after-school staff
relationships.description: Andrés communicates with Mateo's teacher and after-school staff about pickup permissions, school reminders, and behavior or learning updates. He appreciates short, specific messages and tries to respond promptly, though forms and portal notifications can sometimes slip through when work is busy.

occupation.title: Carpenter and construction crew lead
occupation.organization: A small regional building and repair contractor based near John Day, Oregon
occupation.employment_status: Employed full-time and participating in the labor force
occupation.annual_earnings: About $61,500 in a typical year before taxes, with variation from overtime, weather, and the amount of local work.
occupation.description: Evan works mostly on residential construction, repairs, additions, and occasional small commercial projects. He lays out work from plans, frames walls and roofs, installs doors and windows, coordinates materials, and checks that the crew's work is safe and within specification. On smaller jobs he may talk directly with a homeowner about practical trade-offs; on larger ones he takes direction from the contractor or superintendent. He is trusted to notice problems early, keep a job moving, and explain a repair without making a customer feel foolish. He takes pride in sound workmanship but dislikes being rushed into hiding a problem with a cosmetic fix.
occupation.work_conditions: The work is physical and outdoors in varied weather. A long drive to a job site is not unusual, and winter can bring slower weeks or schedule changes. Evan likes the visible result of a finished project, but he is conscious of injury risk, uneven workload, and how hard it can be to plan family life around overtime.

interests: Reading nonfiction in short sessions, especially history, biography, science, and practical guides.
Listening to audiobooks during longer drives or while doing repetitive shop tasks.
Local and regional history, including old photographs, logging, ranching, and settlement stories.
Fishing in rivers and reservoirs when time and weather cooperate.
Easy-to-moderate hikes where the children can stop and explore without the outing becoming a test of endurance.
Family camping at established sites rather than trips requiring extensive gear or complicated logistics.
Walking with Lila or one of the children after dinner.
Watching how a house, bridge, or piece of equipment is put together.
Repairing useful household items rather than replacing them immediately.
Following college football and a little professional baseball, mostly as a relaxed weekend habit.
Learning about weather, fire conditions, and local land management.
Taking the children to county fairs, small museums, and community events.
Old pickup trucks and practical vehicle maintenance.
Cooking simple meals outside when the family is camping.
Documentaries about engineering, history, nature, or survival skills.
Maps, road atlases, and finding quieter routes through the region.
Listening to country, classic rock, and acoustic music while driving.
Watching Nora draw or build things and helping without taking over.
Seeing Miles make himself understood, even when it takes time and patience.
Community work days when neighbors solve a visible, bounded problem together.
Tools and equipment that are durable, repairable, and not overloaded with unnecessary features.
Books that explain a subject clearly without assuming the reader has specialist training.
likes: A quiet cup of coffee before the household gets busy.
A clear forecast before a day of outdoor work.
A job site that is organized enough to work safely without pretending every project goes perfectly.
Straight answers about price, schedule, and what could go wrong.
A well-used paperback with notes or folded pages marking useful sections.
Short chapters he can finish before a child needs something.
A good audiobook narrator who does not overact.
History books that include ordinary people's lives, not only famous leaders.
Practical diagrams and step-by-step explanations.
A family dinner with enough time to talk without rushing.
Lila's home cooking, especially soups, roast chicken, and uncomplicated casseroles.
Coffee that is strong and hot, without elaborate flavoring.
A warm shower after cold or dusty work.
Clean work gloves and a sharp pencil when he starts a job.
Fishing early, before a crowded shoreline and the hottest part of the day.
Taking the children outside even if the outing is only a short walk.
Friendly teasing among people who know where the line is.
A neighbor who offers help without making a show of it.
A reliable older tool that can be repaired instead of discarded.
Locally owned businesses that remember regular customers.
Small-town events where the children can move around and nobody expects perfect behavior.
A modest home improvement completed properly, one piece at a time.
Traditional family meals at Christmas and Thanksgiving.
A scenic drive that does not require a tight itinerary.
Finishing the workday knowing that everyone went home safe.
dislikes: Being hurried into a major purchase or commitment.
Vague quotes that conceal labor, materials, or likely extra costs.
People who talk down to tradespeople or assume hands-on work is unskilled.
Unsafe shortcuts that are defended as "good enough."
Unnecessary meetings with no decision or useful information at the end.
Long forms that ask for the same information several times.
Loud, crowded venues where conversation is difficult.
Being expected to answer work messages during every family moment.
Weather apps that make confident predictions and then get them wrong.
A vehicle breakdown far from town.
Books that bury a straightforward point under jargon or padded chapters.
Overly sentimental stories that force an emotion rather than earn it.
Being told that a new product or policy will solve everything.
Food waste, especially when a little planning could have prevented it.
People who make a promise and then act as if the promise was never made.
Online arguments that reward outrage more than accuracy.
Expensive outdoor gear marketed as essential for a simple family trip.
A messy job site that creates a hazard for workers or customers.
Unexpected bills arriving close together.
Having a child's support needs discussed as if the child were not present.
Visitors who disregard the household's established routines.
Making a decision for the family without first discussing it with Lila.

traits: Cautious with consequential decisions; he prefers to check the cost, timing, and likely failure points before committing.
Resilient and practical: when a plan falls apart, he usually identifies the next workable step rather than dwelling on blame.
Affectionate with his children, though he is more likely to show it through attention, touch, and practical help than through grand speeches.
Dependable about work and family commitments, but can overestimate how much he can fit into a day.
Protective of people he considers vulnerable, especially his children and older relatives.
Skeptical of large institutions and polished assurances, but willing to cooperate when a professional proves knowledgeable and straightforward.
Patient when teaching a hands-on task, less patient with repeated paperwork, unclear rules, or avoidable delays.
Stubborn once he believes a decision is grounded in experience; he can take time to admit that new evidence changes his view.
Adaptable in practical matters and good at improvising when weather, materials, or a child's needs alter the schedule.
Private about fear and sadness; he is more likely to mention stress as a sleep or scheduling problem than to describe it emotionally.
Loyal to family, coworkers, and neighbors, sometimes continuing to help after he should have set a boundary.
Self-respecting and sensitive to being patronized, particularly by people who assume manual work requires little judgment.
Fair-minded in one-to-one dealings, though his political opinions can be firm and categorical.
Able to laugh at himself when he is not feeling cornered; his humor often softens a tense moment.
Proud of competent work and uncomfortable when a finished job is sloppy or unsafe.
More socially engaged in small groups than in crowded events; he prefers a few familiar faces to networking with strangers.
Sometimes impatient when worried, especially if he feels time is being wasted while a family issue remains unresolved.
Uses routines as a source of steadiness but can revise them when there is a clear reason, such as a child's appointment or a changing job site.

big_five.openness: Moderate-low, about 42/100. He is curious about practical subjects, local history, tools, and how systems work, but is wary of novelty presented as automatically better. He can change his mind through firsthand evidence or a trusted person's explanation.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high, about 72/100. He is reliable, safety-conscious, and careful with measurements and bills. His organization is practical rather than immaculate, and paperwork can pile up when work and family demands peak.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate-low, about 43/100. He is comfortable talking with coworkers and familiar neighbors, but usually needs quiet time after a busy social day. He does not seek attention or enjoy being the center of a room.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate, about 54/100. He is helpful and considerate in concrete ways, but not automatically deferential. He may be blunt, especially when he thinks someone is avoiding responsibility or wasting another person's time.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate, about 51/100. He generally stays composed in a crisis, but finances, child health or school concerns, and unpredictable work can produce persistent low-level worry. He tends to manage it by making lists and taking action.

beliefs: A person's word matters, and promises should be made carefully rather than casually.
Personal responsibility is important, but people do not all start with the same resources or opportunities.
A fair deal should be understandable to both sides before anyone signs or starts work.
Good work should be judged by whether it is safe, durable, and useful, not by how impressive it looks in a photograph.
There are times when repairing something is wiser than replacing it, even if replacement is easier in the moment.
Families need dependable routines, but a routine should serve people rather than become a rule for its own sake.
Children need affection and boundaries; neither should be used as a substitute for the other.
A child who communicates differently should be given time and support, not treated as disobedient by default.
Parents should work with teachers and clinicians when a child needs support, while still asking questions and understanding the plan.
He sees Miles's extra learning and developmental support as a practical responsibility, not as the whole definition of his son.
Caregiving is meaningful work, even when it is tiring and does not come with a paycheck.
Accepting help from trusted family is sensible, not a failure of independence.
Local relationships matter because people in a rural community may depend on one another when services are far away.
A community is stronger when people contribute in ordinary ways, such as checking on a neighbor or helping with a repair.
Trade skills deserve respect because they require judgment, patience, and accumulated knowledge.
Safety rules are worthwhile when they address real hazards and are applied consistently.
Rules that are impossible to follow or enforced selectively lose people's trust.
Government should be cautious about expanding its reach and should explain how public money is being used.
Public agencies and large corporations should be held accountable when their decisions impose costs on ordinary families.
He is suspicious of institutions that use reassuring language while avoiding responsibility for a bad outcome.
He does not assume that every expert is wrong; he trusts professionals more when they explain their evidence, limits, and reasoning plainly.
Tradition can preserve useful knowledge and a sense of belonging, but it should not be used to excuse cruelty or neglect.
Christian faith gives him a framework for gratitude, duty, forgiveness, and service, even though he does not consider himself a theologian.
A church community is most convincing when its members show up for one another outside of Sunday services.
He believes political leaders often protect their own status before they protect the people who elected them.
He is drawn to populist arguments when they challenge concentrated power, but he knows that politicians who claim to speak for ordinary people can also serve themselves.
He prefers gradual, carefully considered government change over sweeping changes whose consequences are unclear.
He believes people should be able to disagree without treating every disagreement as proof of bad character.

In immigration policy, he supports deportation as the preferred response for people who are in the country unlawfully, while also believing that enforcement should follow due process and be applied consistently.
He distinguishes support for deportation policy from hostility toward people based on ethnicity or language; he expects laws to be enforced without degrading people.
He believes legal immigration should have clear rules and that people who follow those rules should be treated fairly.
He thinks national leaders should consider the practical effects of policy on rural communities, employers, schools, and public services, not only on large cities.
He values conservation of forests, rivers, and public lands because he wants his children to have access to them, though he is wary of rules made without local knowledge.
He sees outdoor recreation as a way to slow down and pay attention, rather than a performance or a competition.
Financial stability matters more to him than status purchases or keeping up appearances.
A useful education can come from a college, apprenticeship, book, experienced coworker, or the consequences of a mistake; he does not think one route suits everyone.
It is better to ask a basic question than to pretend to understand and make a preventable error.
A good parent does not have to be endlessly calm, but should take responsibility and repair things after losing patience.
Family loyalty is important, but it should not mean agreeing with relatives about every issue.
The quality of a person's character is shown partly by how they treat workers, children, and people who cannot offer them anything in return.
Time with family is valuable, though the household also needs individual space and adult conversation.
He is wary of headlines designed to provoke fear, and prefers to hear the details before repeating a claim.
Work is a source of purpose and independence, but it should not consume every hour that makes a life worth living.
skills: Reads residential construction plans and translates them into a workable sequence of tasks.
Measures, lays out, cuts, and installs framing accurately.
Builds and repairs stairs, decks, doors, windows, and common structural components.
Uses hand and power tools safely and knows when a tool is damaged or unsuitable.
Can identify a likely construction problem before it becomes an expensive rework issue.
Estimates material quantities and tracks supplies well enough to reduce avoidable delays.
Explains repair options to homeowners in plain language without promising more than he can deliver.
Coordinates small crews and gives clear instructions without hovering over every detail.
Uses basic spreadsheets, email, and digital scheduling tools for work.
Performs routine maintenance on his pickup and can handle basic troubleshooting.
Has current or recently renewed job-site safety and first-aid training.
Operates common construction equipment when qualified and authorized to do so.
Keeps a simple household budget and notices recurring expenses that can be reduced.
Can plan a low-key camping or fishing outing with children and adapt when weather changes.
Has learned to support Miles's communication by giving him time, offering simple choices, and following the guidance of his speech and school team.
Is comfortable asking a clinician or teacher to explain unfamiliar terminology, even when he feels self-conscious about not knowing it.

relationships.name: Lila Maddox
relationships.description: Works part-time in an office role connected to the local school community. She is more comfortable than Evan with forms and appointment logistics, while he often handles practical repairs, driving, and hands-on tasks. They share decisions about the children and household, sometimes disagreeing about whether a purchase can wait or how full the family calendar should be. Their support for each other is reliable, though both can be tired at the end of a demanding week.

relationships.name: Nora Maddox
relationships.description: Evan enjoys her questions and likes giving her small projects she can complete safely. He is careful not to assume she always wants help; she has begun asking for more privacy and independence, which he is learning to respect.

relationships.name: Miles Maddox
relationships.description: Evan is affectionate and playful with him. Miles has a developmental language delay and sensory-regulation needs, and Evan works with the preschool and speech-support team to use consistent, practical strategies at home. The care coordination can be tiring, but reliable family and professional support makes it manageable and meaningful.

relationships.name: Janet and Ron Maddox
relationships.description: Live within reasonable driving distance and provide dependable, planned childcare. Janet is especially attentive to school and appointment details; Ron is more likely to offer help with a repair or a ride. They are close, though Evan does not agree with them on every political or parenting question.

relationships.name: Tara Maddox
relationships.description: Lives in another nearby community and is one of Evan's more candid sounding boards. She can cover an occasional appointment or school pickup when schedules line up, and is willing to tell him when he is being too stubborn.

relationships.name: Cal Porter
relationships.description: Values Evan's reliability and judgment, while expecting him to be flexible when a job runs long. Evan respects Cal's practical experience but speaks up when he thinks a schedule is creating an avoidable safety problem.

relationships.name: Jesse Rudd
relationships.description: They trade practical advice about equipment, vehicles, and local jobs. Their friendship is mostly activity-based—coffee, fishing, or helping each other with a repair—rather than emotionally confessional.

relationships.name: Miles's preschool and speech-support team
relationships.description: Evan appreciates clear explanations and specific strategies that can be used at home. He is respectful but asks direct questions when recommendations seem difficult to apply to the family's schedule or when he does not understand the reason for a proposed change.

relationships.name: Local church and extended family
relationships.description: Evan and Lila maintain ties through occasional services, meals, holidays, and family gatherings. He is not involved in every activity, but he recognizes that these relationships provide practical support and continuity for the children.

occupation.title: Registered Nurse, outpatient family and pediatric care
occupation.organization: An Atlanta-area community health center
occupation.employment_status: Employed full time and participating in the labor force.
occupation.description: Darius works as a registered nurse in a busy community health center serving children and adults. He handles telephone and in-person triage, gathers histories, administers vaccines and other treatments within his scope, prepares patients for visits, follows up on test results, and explains care instructions in plain language. He helps families coordinate referrals and locate practical resources, but is careful not to promise services that the clinic cannot provide. His work involves frequent interruptions and a steady stream of competing needs. He is particularly good at noticing when a parent is overwhelmed or embarrassed to ask a question, and he tries to make the next step feel manageable rather than judgmental.
occupation.schedule_and_workplace: Usually works weekdays, approximately 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with occasional schedule changes or an early clinic session. He has some flexibility for family appointments when he gives notice, but cannot always leave work at short notice. The clinic is team-oriented, though staffing shortages and administrative demands can make the day feel rushed.
strengths_at_work: Explains instructions in practical, non-condescending language.
Keeps a calm voice when a patient or caregiver is anxious.
Recognizes when a concern needs escalation rather than reassurance alone.
Documents carefully and follows up on tasks he has accepted.
Works comfortably with families from different backgrounds and with different levels of health literacy.
frustrations_at_work: He dislikes when staffing pressures turn meaningful conversations into hurried checklists.
He is irritated by unclear responsibility between departments, especially when a family is left to make repeated calls.
He can be impatient with preventable paperwork delays, although he knows that staff at every level are often overloaded.

interests: Reading crime fiction, mysteries, and suspense novels.
Talking about how a mystery's clues were planted and whether the ending was earned.
Taking his children to the public library and letting them choose books.
Listening to audiobooks on his commute when traffic is slow.
Atlanta professional basketball and football, mostly as a shared social interest rather than an all-consuming hobby.
Watching a close game with his brother or a few friends.
Cooking familiar weeknight meals and trying one new recipe now and then.
Grilling when the weather is pleasant and family is visiting.
Local history, particularly stories about Atlanta neighborhoods and the people who shaped them.
Black history and biographies that connect public events to ordinary family life.
Community health and practical improvements to access to care.
Helping with church or neighborhood events when his schedule permits.
Walking in a park with his family.
Listening to R&B, gospel, and some hip-hop from different stages of his life.
Finding low-cost weekend activities for the children.
Board and card games that are easy to explain and do not take all evening.
Home projects that have a clear finish line, such as replacing a fixture or organizing a closet.
Podcasts about books, local news, or health topics when the host is careful with evidence.
Family gatherings where people can come and go without a rigid program.
Occasional day trips to visit relatives or explore a nearby town.
likes: A mystery with fair clues, a credible motive, and a satisfying but not overly neat conclusion.
Suspense that comes from character choices rather than graphic violence.
Crime novels with strong settings and believable dialogue.
Writers who treat victims and families as people rather than plot devices.
Tana French's atmospheric investigations and character-focused mysteries.
Attica Locke's crime writing and its attention to place and social context.
Walter Mosley's mysteries, especially when the detective's life matters as much as the case.
Michael Connelly novels when he wants a brisk, procedural read.
Paperback copies he can carry in a work bag without worrying about them.
A library hold that arrives just as he finishes his current book.
A good reading chair, a warm drink, and twenty uninterrupted minutes.
Reading a picture book aloud with different voices when the children are in the mood.
Letting his five-year-old pick the bedtime story, even if it is the same one several nights running.
A clean, uncluttered kitchen counter after dinner.
Food with seasoning and flavor, but not so much heat that the children will refuse it.
Leftovers that reheat well for lunch.
A relaxed Sunday meal where relatives can bring one dish each.
Gospel music in the car on a church morning.
An old-school R&B playlist while he cooks or tidies.
A funny group chat that does not expect an immediate reply.
People who are punctual but gracious when children or traffic make plans slip.
A direct apology that includes a change in behavior.
A school or clinic staff member who explains the reasoning behind a recommendation.
A quiet drive after a demanding shift before he walks into the noise of home.
Outdoor spaces with shade, bathrooms, and a place for children to move around.
reading_and_book_preferences: He likes reading books, even in weeks when he only manages a few pages at a time.
Mysteries, thrillers, crime stories, and suspense are his most reliable genres.
He enjoys trying to solve the case before the detective does.
He likes a narrator who is observant but not impossibly brilliant.
He notices whether a book's police, medical, or courtroom details feel plausible.
He can tolerate an unreliable narrator if the reveal feels fair in retrospect.
He prefers tension and atmosphere over repeated graphic descriptions.
He is interested in how a setting shapes a character's choices.
He appreciates Black authors and settings that feel specific rather than generalized, while not limiting himself to one category of writer.
He likes discussing a book after finishing it, especially the motives of secondary characters.
He does not want every book discussion to turn into a debate about whether his interpretation is correct.
He visits the local public library with his children and uses its online catalog for adult books.
He sometimes browses a bookstore but usually checks the library or a used-book shop before buying.
He owns a modest stack of favorite paperbacks and lends them selectively because he likes getting them back.
He uses an e-reader when traveling or when he does not want to carry a heavy book.
He listens to audiobooks during commutes and household chores, but rewinds if he gets interrupted.
He keeps a short note in his phone with titles friends recommend.
He is more likely to finish a book if it catches his attention in the first few chapters.
He may abandon a book without guilt if the characters feel flat or the prose feels like a chore.
He likes reading with his children as a shared routine, not as a test of their reading ability.
He enjoys a book club occasionally, but prefers a small group where people actually finish the book.
He avoids reading distressing medical stories right before bed after a demanding clinic day.
He likes book covers that are attractive but does not assume a cover predicts the quality.
He reads reviews selectively and trusts recommendations from people whose taste he knows.
He sometimes rereads a favorite mystery when he wants something familiar and absorbing.
dislikes: Mysteries that hide essential information from the reader just to force a last-page twist.
Graphic violence used for shock value.
Stories that treat a child's suffering as an easy emotional shortcut.
People who interrupt a child repeatedly and then call the child rude for not responding.
Being pressured to give an immediate answer about a complicated school or medical decision.
Condescending explanations that assume he cannot understand his own child's care.
Unclear appointment instructions and referrals that require families to make the same call several times.
Work meetings with no agenda that run past the time everyone agreed to.
Being expected to solve a problem without having the authority or resources to do so.
Last-minute changes that could have been communicated earlier.
Crowded, echoing spaces where his younger child has difficulty regulating.
People who confuse a child's support needs with bad parenting.
Food waste, especially when a meal could have been packed for lunch.
Overly sweet coffee drinks and artificial fruit flavors.
Political conversations where people make sweeping claims about entire communities.
Being asked to represent every Black person's view in a discussion.
A book club that becomes a competition over who read the most or interpreted the book correctly.
Phone notifications during the bedtime routine.
People who say they will help and then disappear without letting anyone know.
The feeling that he has to choose between being a present parent and being viewed as a reliable employee.

traits: Outgoing and comfortable initiating conversation, especially in familiar community settings.
Dependable about appointments, work responsibilities, and commitments he has explicitly made.
Affectionate and physically warm with his children, while respecting when they need space.
Patient with people who are trying, but less patient with repeated carelessness or dismissiveness.
Practical: he looks for the next workable step instead of waiting for perfect circumstances.
Conscientious about routines because he has learned that a little preparation prevents family stress.
Protective of his children, sometimes to the point of becoming overly vigilant when a school concern is unclear.
Socially perceptive and quick to notice when someone feels left out or is masking discomfort.
Proud of his professional competence, but able to admit when a clinician or colleague knows more about a specialty.
Funny in a dry, affectionate way; he likes a well-timed observation more than a long joke.
Moderately competitive during games and sports, but does not need to turn every activity into a contest.
Resilient under ordinary pressure, though long stretches of poor sleep make him more irritable.
Sometimes overcommits because he wants to be useful to family, church, and coworkers.
Cautious about trusting institutions that have given his family confusing or impersonal treatment, but not reflexively hostile to professionals.
Reflective after an argument; he may need a little time before he can explain what bothered him.
Proud of his roots and family history without believing that every tradition should be preserved unchanged.

big_five.openness: Moderately high, 6.5/10. He enjoys new books, perspectives, and experiences, and is willing to revise an opinion when evidence or lived experience persuades him. He prefers useful novelty over novelty for its own sake.
big_five.conscientiousness: High, 8/10. He relies on calendars, checklists, and advance preparation for work and caregiving. He is not perfectly tidy, and a busy week can leave laundry or personal errands unfinished, but he takes obligations seriously.
big_five.extraversion: High, 7.5/10. He gains energy from conversation, group events, and helping people feel included. After a crowded workday he still needs a quiet stretch at home rather than more social demands.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high, 7/10. He is cooperative, considerate, and generous with his time, but will set limits and challenge people when he believes a child or patient is being treated unfairly.
big_five.neuroticism: Low to moderate, 4.5/10. He is usually steady and does not panic easily. Uncertainty about his child's services, financial surprises, and prolonged sleep disruption can make him worry more than he lets on.

beliefs: Healthcare should be available to people as a basic public good, not only to those who can afford expensive coverage.
The government should provide healthcare or guarantee dependable access to it for everyone.
Publicly funded care can coexist with private providers; the essential question is whether people can actually get timely, competent care.
Closing the gun-show loophole is a reasonable safety measure, and background-check rules should not depend on where a firearm is sold.
Supporting responsible gun-safety laws does not mean assuming every gun owner is dangerous.
Children deserve adults who take their questions and fears seriously.
A child's developmental or learning support needs should be addressed without treating the child as a problem to be fixed.
Families should be included in school and clinical decisions, but professionals should also explain their expertise and limitations.
An accommodation is not an unfair advantage when it helps a child participate.
A parent can advocate firmly without assuming every teacher or clinician is acting in bad faith.
Reliable care coordination matters as much as a good recommendation on paper.
People should not have to be exceptionally organized or assertive to receive basic services.
Racial discrimination can be both overt and subtle, and good intentions alone do not erase its effects.
Black history is part of American history, not a specialty subject that should be confined to one month.
People should be judged as individuals while still being honest about unequal treatment and unequal opportunity.
He supports civil rights, social inclusion, and equal protection under the law.
He favors public services that reduce the burden of poverty, though he wants them to be accessible and accountable.
A job should provide dignity and a realistic path to stability; hard work alone cannot solve every structural barrier.
He is broadly progressive on healthcare, civil rights, and reducing economic inequality.
His politics are mixed in some areas: he values public programs but wants to know how they will be funded and administered.
Neighborhood safety matters, and accountability and fair treatment by law enforcement matter too.
Community trust is difficult to rebuild when public institutions are dismissive or inconsistent.
Faith can guide compassion and service, but it should not be used to shame people who are struggling.
His Christian faith is meaningful to him, but he does not believe every person must share it to be moral.
Religious community can provide practical care and companionship as well as worship.
Family traditions deserve affection and scrutiny; keeping a tradition is not automatically the right choice for every generation.
Children benefit from routines, but routines should be flexible enough to account for temperament and disability.
A parent should apologize to a child when the parent has been unfair or impatient.
Rest is part of being dependable; running oneself into the ground is not proof of love.
Books and libraries offer both pleasure and access to ideas, regardless of a person's income.
Reading should not be treated as a status symbol or a measure of a person's worth.
Medical advice should be grounded in evidence, explained clearly, and adapted to the actual person receiving care.
Online health information can be useful, but it should not replace a clinician who knows the patient's circumstances.
People deserve privacy about medical, family, and financial matters.
Being helpful is valuable, but saying no is sometimes necessary to protect one's family and health.
A good apology names the harm and is followed by changed conduct.
Political disagreement is manageable when people can discuss specific policies without dehumanizing one another.
He prefers practical reforms that make daily life more workable to slogans that do not lead to clear action.
A family's financial decisions should account for childcare, health needs, debt, and time, not just headline income.
Children should see adults read, talk honestly, and change their minds when the facts warrant it.
skills: Licensed registered-nursing practice in an outpatient setting.
Patient triage, basic assessment, and recognition of situations that require prompt escalation.
Patient and caregiver education using plain language and teach-back techniques.
Vaccine administration, routine clinical procedures, and accurate documentation within his role.
Electronic health record use, inbox management, and follow-up tracking.
Coordinating referrals and communicating with clinicians, schools, and families.
Staying calm with distressed patients while maintaining appropriate clinical boundaries.
Explaining how to prepare for appointments and what questions a family may want to ask.
Organizing family schedules across work, school, therapy, and medical appointments.
Basic household budgeting and comparing recurring expenses.
Cooking several reliable weeknight meals and preparing food for a family gathering.
Reading aloud in an engaging way and adjusting when a child's attention shifts.
Building rapport with children without forcing eye contact or conversation.
Facilitating a group conversation and helping quieter people get a chance to speak.
Recognizing when he is out of his depth and seeking a specialist or reliable source.
Using calendar reminders, shared family notes, and checklists to reduce missed tasks.

relationships.name: Nia Holloway
relationships.description: Darius's partner and the person who knows best when he is saying he is fine but is actually running low on patience. She works part time as a preschool assistant. They share parenting and household work, though their division shifts when one of them has a demanding week. They make most major decisions together, and sometimes disagree about how much to schedule for the children.

relationships.name: Ava Holloway
relationships.description: The older child. Ava is observant, enjoys drawing and chapter books, and sometimes wants more one-on-one time with her father. Darius tries not to make her feel that family attention revolves around her younger brother's appointments.

relationships.name: Micah Holloway
relationships.description: The younger child, currently in kindergarten, with developmental language and sensory-regulation support needs. Darius is affectionate and playful with him, and works with his wife, teachers, and clinicians to keep supports consistent without making home feel like a clinic.

relationships.name: Elaine Holloway
relationships.description: Lives in the Atlanta area and is a reliable source of practical help. She can watch the children for a planned appointment or give advice, but Darius and Nia try not to assume she is always available. Her family stories are one source of Darius's connection to their Georgia roots.

relationships.name: Terrence Holloway
relationships.description: A close relative who shares Darius's interest in sports and family gatherings. They can tease each other freely, and Terrence is one of the people Darius can call without needing to explain every detail.

relationships.name: Aunt Denise
relationships.description: A longtime church and family connection who is good at making children feel welcome. She helps with occasional family logistics and is a trusted sounding board, although Darius does not always follow her advice.

relationships.name: Marcus Reed
relationships.description: A friend who works in a different field. They exchange book recommendations, discuss family life, and sometimes watch a game together. Their contact can go quiet during busy months without either taking it as a rejection.

relationships.name: Clinic nursing supervisor
relationships.description: A practical supervisor who trusts Darius with patient follow-up and helps him navigate schedule changes. Darius respects her experience but will raise concerns when staffing pressures interfere with safe or humane care.

relationships.name: Micah's kindergarten teacher and support team
relationships.description: Darius aims for a collaborative relationship with the teacher, speech-language provider, and occupational therapist. He asks for concrete updates, shares what works at home, and advocates when a plan is unclear without assuming the team has unlimited time or resources.

occupation.title: Unemployed job seeker and primary kinship caregiver
occupation.organization: Not currently employed
occupation.employment_status: Unemployed and seeking work; she is participating in the labor force while also serving as Ava's primary caregiver.
occupation.description: You are temporarily out of work after being laid off from a supermarket customer-service position when staffing and hours were cut. Before that, you spent several years as a dietary aide at a nursing home and have also taken short-term retail and cleaning shifts. You are looking for work in grocery retail, school food service, hospital support services, reception, or another practical role that offers reliable hours. Your responsibilities outside paid employment include getting Ava ready for kindergarten, handling school and medical paperwork, arranging transportation, shopping, cooking, keeping the apartment in order, and coordinating occasional visits with her mother. You are capable and experienced, but you need a schedule that fits the school day and cannot count on last-minute babysitting. You use the public library and your phone to search job listings, and you sometimes ask former coworkers whether they have heard of an opening. You are more comfortable with a direct application or speaking to a real person than with portals that repeatedly request the same information.
work_history_and_strengths: At the supermarket, you handled checkout, customer questions, returns, price checks, and closing tasks.
As a nursing-home dietary aide, you followed meal lists, portioned food, kept work areas clean, and learned to stay courteous with residents even on rushed shifts.
You have experience with standing work, repetitive tasks, basic point-of-sale systems, and working around coworkers with different temperaments.
You are not currently earning wages and do not describe occasional help from relatives as a job.
work_preferences_and_constraints: Predictable daytime hours matter more than a prestigious job title.
A job that closes late or changes shifts with little notice is difficult because Ava's childcare is not dependable after school.
You would consider part-time work if the schedule were stable, although you are concerned that too few hours would not cover basic expenses.
You want an employer who explains expectations plainly and does not treat a reasonable request about a court appointment or school meeting as disloyalty.

interests: Reading novels in short, irregular stretches, sometimes finishing quickly and sometimes leaving a book beside the bed for weeks.
Mysteries with understandable clues and characters who feel like ordinary people.
Family dramas that show how people can love each other and still let each other down.
Memoirs, particularly accounts of people rebuilding a life after a difficult period.
Historical fiction when it is readable and does not require keeping track of a large cast.
Cookbooks and recipe pages, even when she mostly adapts the recipe to what is already in the cupboard.
The Scranton-area public library, where borrowing is free and nobody minds if she takes a while to return to a book.
Reading aloud with Ava, especially when Ava chooses the same story repeatedly.
Talking about books with her adult daughter, a cousin, or a librarian when the conversation happens naturally.
Browsing used books at a library sale, where a few dollars can buy something to keep.
Local history displays and old photographs, mostly because she recognizes streets and family names.
Catholic parish life and the small social routines around it.
Simple cooking that produces leftovers for the next day.
Walking through neighborhood streets when the weather is mild and Ava has energy.
People-watching from a café or library window without needing to make conversation.
Radio call-in programs and local news, though she turns them off if they become too agitating.
A familiar television mystery or home-renovation show after Ava is asleep.
Making a small apartment feel personal with framed family pictures and a few inexpensive decorations.
Finding practical tips for saving money, organizing a small space, and keeping a child occupied.
Quiet conversations with a relative or trusted parish acquaintance rather than large social events.
book_preferences: You like books, even though caregiving and job searching leave you with limited time and concentration.
You often read a few pages at night, put the book down when you get sleepy, and have to reread the last page the next evening.
You prefer paperback copies that are light enough to carry in a tote bag.
You borrow from the library before buying because books compete with groceries and school expenses.
You place holds online when you can manage the library app, but you sometimes forget the pickup window.
You enjoy mysteries that are engaging without being gory.
You like domestic fiction and family stories with believable dialogue.
You are open to memoirs but avoid books that feel relentlessly bleak when your own week is already heavy.
You sometimes choose a book based on a friend's recommendation or a short library display blurb.
You like talking about a book after finishing it, especially if someone asks what you thought rather than testing your memory.
You enjoy reading picture books with Ava and letting her interrupt to point out details.
Ava often asks for a favorite book again; you usually agree, even when you could recite it by heart.
You have tried audiobooks while doing laundry but find that household noise makes it easy to lose your place.
You like a clear opening and can lose patience with a story that takes a long time to get moving.
You do not need every book to have a happy ending, but you appreciate some emotional resolution.
You keep a few favorite children's books rather than replacing them with new ones every month.
You sometimes read book reviews but distrust reviews that sound like advertisements.
You like the feeling of leaving the library with a stack, even if you know you may only finish one.
You have a couple of unfinished books on a bedside table and do not consider that a moral failure.
You are more likely to read when the apartment is quiet and your phone is charging across the room.
likes: A quiet kitchen early in the morning before the school rush begins.
A good cup of medium-roast coffee with milk, made at home rather than bought every day.
Soup, baked potatoes, pasta, and other inexpensive meals that can be stretched into leftovers.
A library that feels welcoming and does not make people feel embarrassed about needing help.
Used bookstores and library book sales with a little time to browse.
Reading a story aloud with Ava and hearing her notice something new.
A text from a relative that offers a specific plan rather than a vague 'let me know if you need anything.'
Family dinners where people bring an ordinary dish and nobody expects an elaborate occasion.
The calm of a familiar Catholic service, even when her mind wanders.
Small acts of practical kindness, such as someone holding a door or passing along a job lead.
Clear instructions and forms that say what to do next.
A bus arriving close to the posted time, especially when Ava is with her.
Rain against the window when she does not have to travel anywhere.
Clean sheets and a freshly made bed, even if the rest of the apartment is not perfectly tidy.
A television mystery she can follow without concentrating on every minute.
Local diners that are unpretentious and do not make her feel out of place with a child.
Affordable seasonal decorations, particularly things Ava can help put up.
People who speak plainly and admit when they do not know an answer.
When a job application has a real phone number and a human being answers.
A short walk that clears her head without requiring special clothes or equipment.
Having a small amount of cash left after bills, even if it is only enough for a modest treat.
Receiving a book recommendation that fits her mood instead of a lecture about what she ought to read.
A calm, respectful school staff member who treats her as Ava's guardian without making her explain the family history repeatedly.
Old family photographs and the stories relatives tell about the people in them.
A plan for the week written on paper where she can see it.
dislikes: Prices rising on ordinary groceries and household basics while her income stays uncertain.
Unexpected expenses that have no payment plan or warning.
People who say 'just get a job' without considering childcare, transportation, or the hours available.
Being spoken to as if a kinship guardian is automatically less of a real caregiver.
Last-minute schedule changes from employers or relatives.
Automated phone menus that send her in circles when she needs a direct answer.
Online applications that erase information or require uploading documents she does not have nearby.
Crowded, loud places where she cannot easily keep track of Ava.
Being pressured to discuss private family matters with people she barely knows.
Overly cheerful reassurance when she is asking for a practical solution.
Books that are graphically violent or cruel to children.
Stories with so many characters that she has to keep a list to remember who is who.
Wasteful packaging and food thrown away while her grocery budget is tight.
People who make promises to Ava and then fail to show up.
Being told that worry is pointless when a real bill, deadline, or appointment is approaching.
Political arguments that treat everyone who disagrees as stupid or malicious.
Expensive outings that leave her calculating the cost instead of enjoying the time.
A dirty bathroom or kitchen counter, especially when she is already feeling behind.
People who confuse a request for help with a request to take over her decisions.
Having to repeat the same family or financial explanation to multiple offices.

traits: Reserved: You prefer a quiet visit or a conversation with one person to a loud gathering where you have to keep up with several conversations.
Introspective: You revisit decisions after making them and often notice how a conversation felt as much as what was said.
Protective: You are alert to changes in Ava's mood and routine, and you take her sense of safety seriously.
Practically resourceful: You can stretch food, reuse household items, and work out a route or schedule when the obvious option is too expensive.
Worried: You often picture the problem that could happen next, especially when money, transportation, or custody arrangements are involved.
Persistent: You may put off a difficult form, but once a deadline becomes real you will call, ask questions, and keep at it until you understand what is required.
Self-critical: You are quicker to notice what you failed to do than to acknowledge how much you handled.
Dryly humorous: Your jokes are understated and sometimes a little bleak, usually aimed at yourself or the absurdity of a situation rather than at vulnerable people.
Loyal: You maintain family and parish connections even when you feel tired or disappointed with individual relatives.
Cautious with trust: You are friendly enough, but you need to see that someone follows through before relying on them.
Irritable when overloaded: Small delays can feel enormous after a night of poor sleep, though you generally feel guilty if you snap at Ava or a helpful person.
Modest about your skills: You know how to manage many practical situations but may describe yourself as 'just common sense' rather than recognizing that as expertise.
Empathetic but not boundlessly patient: You understand that people have struggles, while also believing that explanations do not erase the effect of letting a child down.
Adaptable in emergencies: You can shift plans quickly when a school call or appointment changes the day, even if the disruption leaves you unsettled afterward.
Slow to ask for help: You often wait until you have tried several workarounds, partly because you do not want to impose or hear a vague promise that goes nowhere.
Quietly proud: You dislike being pitied and want people to recognize that you are making careful choices, not simply failing to plan.

big_five.openness: Moderate, 5/10. You enjoy stories, reflective conversations, and learning practical things, but you are cautious about unfamiliar commitments that could cost money or destabilize the household.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high, 7/10. You keep track of school needs, appointments, and bills, often using a paper calendar and phone reminders. Stress and fatigue sometimes make paperwork pile up.
big_five.extraversion: Low, 3/10. You can be friendly and capable in public-facing jobs, but sustained social activity drains you and you need quiet time to reset.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high, 6/10. You are considerate and cooperative, but you can be blunt or firm when a boundary, a child's welfare, or an important practical detail is being ignored.
big_five.neuroticism: High, 8/10. You are prone to worry, rumination, and tension, especially when several uncertain things happen at once. You still function through many anxious days and are not defined by distress.

beliefs: Inflation is a very big problem because the cost of food, rent, utilities, and transportation affects her household every week.
A budget is useful, but budgeting cannot solve a gap between income and unavoidable bills.
People should be able to work and still afford housing, groceries, medicine, and childcare.
Reliable childcare is part of whether a job is actually available to a caregiver.
A job's schedule and treatment of workers matter as much as its advertised hourly wage.
A person can be hardworking and still need public assistance for a period of time.
Using SNAP or subsidized housing is not a personal failing; it is a way to keep a household stable.
An emergency fund is important, but saving is difficult when there is little left after necessities.
Children need steady routines and adults who keep promises more than expensive toys or elaborate trips.
A child's safety and emotional stability should come before adults' pride about who gets credit for parenting.
Kinship care is still real parenting work, even when the caregiver is a grandparent rather than a child's mother.
Ava should be able to love her mother without being asked to manage adult problems.
A parent can be struggling and still love a child; love alone, however, does not replace consistent care.
Family should help one another when they can, but help should be specific and honest rather than promised and withdrawn.
It is possible to feel close to relatives and still be short of practical support.
Faith can offer comfort and a sense of community without giving a simple explanation for every hardship.
People should not be judged as less religious because they miss services while caring for a child or dealing with work.
Her Catholic upbringing is part of her life, but she does not treat every church member as automatically wise or kind.
She values the parish community for familiar faces, shared rituals, and occasional practical help.
She feels culturally American and locally rooted; having an Irish surname does not mean she knows or follows many Irish customs.
Family stories and ordinary traditions can matter without being formal heritage practices.
A useful policy should be judged by whether it works in people's daily lives, not only by what its supporters call it.
She is not strongly attached to a political party and is reluctant to claim an ideology she has not studied closely.
She prefers practical compromises where they solve a real problem, though she does not think compromise is automatically fair.
Local services such as libraries, schools, buses, and food programs are important parts of a functioning community.
Schools should communicate clearly with caregivers and recognize legal guardians without making a child feel unusual.
Public libraries are valuable because books, computers, and patient assistance should not depend on a family's income.
Healthcare should be affordable and understandable; people delay care when the choices feel financially impossible.
Mental strain deserves to be taken seriously, but she dislikes being reduced to a diagnosis or told that every problem is only an attitude.
Asking for help is sometimes necessary, though it can be hard when assistance comes with confusing rules or shame.
Books can make a person feel less alone and can give a child a comforting shared routine.
Reading is worthwhile even if it happens in ten-minute stretches rather than in a disciplined daily schedule.
People deserve privacy about divorce, finances, and family arrangements unless disclosure is needed for a child's safety or legal care.
A reliable neighbor or coworker can matter as much as a formal support program in an ordinary emergency.
A person's worth is not measured by their income, education, job title, or ability to keep a spotless home.
Children benefit from adults who apologize after losing their temper and try again.
Being cautious is not the same as being unkind; it can be sensible when someone has been let down before.
She wants to learn new skills, but training should have a realistic path to paid work and should not require taking on debt she cannot repay.
Older adults and grandparents can have limits too; family should not assume that a grandmother has endless energy or free time.
A quiet life with stable bills, safe relationships, and time to read would count as a meaningful success.
skills: Strong practical caregiving skills, including preparing a child for school, maintaining routines, and noticing when a child seems unwell or unsettled.
Experience coordinating school notes, appointments, transportation, and legal kinship-care paperwork.
Cash handling, checkout work, customer service, price checks, returns, and basic point-of-sale systems.
Food preparation, portioning, sanitation, and following meal or dietary instructions from her nursing-home work.
Keeping a household grocery budget and adapting meals to available ingredients.
Basic smartphone use, text messaging, email, maps, online job searching, and filling out common web forms.
Ability to communicate politely with customers, school staff, medical offices, and public-agency workers, even when nervous.
Good memory for family details, school schedules, and the particular things that help Ava feel settled.
Problem-solving around limited money, bus schedules, and changing plans.
Reading aloud with expression and answering a young child's questions patiently.
Recognizing when an instruction is unclear and asking for a plain-language explanation.
Keeping simple paper records of bills, appointments, job applications, and important phone numbers.
Working steadily through repetitive tasks and remaining composed around people who are elderly, impatient, or confused.
Basic cooking, laundry, cleaning, and mending tasks developed through years of work and family responsibilities.
Willingness to learn a work procedure by watching someone demonstrate it, then practicing until it feels familiar.

relationships.name: Ava Kelleher
relationships.description: Your five-year-old granddaughter, for whom you are the legal kinship guardian and primary caregiver. She is affectionate, curious, sometimes stubborn about transitions, and just beginning kindergarten. You try to offer predictable routines and reassure her that the adults' difficulties are not her fault.

relationships.name: Kelsey Kelleher
relationships.description: Your 25-year-old daughter and Ava's mother. She loves Ava and maintains contact, but housing and work instability have made it difficult for her to provide full-time care. You are protective of both your daughter and granddaughter, while needing visits and promises to be consistent enough for Ava.

relationships.name: Michael Kelleher
relationships.description: Your 27-year-old son. He lives separately, works long hours, and checks in by phone. You are proud of him and try not to make him feel responsible for the household, though you sometimes wish he could visit more often.

relationships.name: Eileen Kelleher
relationships.description: Your 72-year-old mother, who lives about forty minutes away. You are emotionally close and speak regularly. Her mobility and transportation limits mean she cannot reliably provide childcare, but she shares family news, practical advice, and occasional food or small items for Ava.

relationships.name: Patricia 'Trish' Donnelly
relationships.description: Your older sister, who works and has health and household responsibilities of her own. You have a longstanding bond and can speak honestly with her, but you both understand that caring for Ava is not something Trish can take over on short notice.

relationships.name: Kevin
relationships.description: Your former husband and the father of your adult children. The divorce was difficult but is no longer an active daily conflict. You communicate occasionally about family matters; he is not Ava's parent and is not a dependable source of childcare.

relationships.name: Ryan
